What makes a Superhost?

The project

For Northwestern’s STAT 303-3 machine learning competition, I modeled Superhost status using anonymized listings from Chicago, Asheville, and Kauai. The task was to submit probabilities, with ROC-AUC as the competition metric.

The training data included 5,510 listings, with 57 columns including the target; the test set contained 3,308 listings. Features mixed prices, reviews, availability, property categories, text, and boolean flags. My final CatBoost submission placed second among 124 participants with a ROC-AUC of 0.9908.

My role
Data cleaning, feature engineering, model comparison, and final submission
Context
STAT 303-3: Data Science with Python III
Evaluation
Competition ROC-AUC; 5-fold stratified validation

Making mixed listing data usable

Clean the fields

I handled inconsistent currency and percentage formats, missing values, and categorical encodings before fitting the models.

Engineer features

Amenities, descriptions, host behavior, and availability offered ways to turn raw listing fields into model inputs.

Compare models

I explored Random Forest, bagged trees, decision trees, AdaBoost, XGBoost, and a stacked ensemble. CatBoost gave the best validation performance and produced the final probabilities.

How it works

The pipeline moved from raw listing fields to probability estimates. Five-fold stratified cross-validation preserved class balance while guiding model selection and tuning.

  1. Prepare listings

    Clean formats, impute missing data, and construct useful numeric and categorical features.

  2. Validate models

    Tune candidate models using five stratified folds and compare their ROC-AUC.

  3. Submit probabilities

    Use the tuned CatBoost classifier to predict Superhost probabilities for the held-out test listings.

The published final configuration uses 500 estimators, a 0.05 learning rate, depth 8, and class weighting. The notebook contains the implementation and tuning work.

A key decision

Choose the model through comparison.

I did not start and end with one classifier. Comparing tree-based models and ensembles helped establish whether extra complexity improved validation performance.

CatBoost was the final choice after those comparisons. The reported 0.9908 is the competition score, and the linked report lets visitors inspect the preprocessing and modeling choices behind it.

Model details

The three markets

Chicago, Illinois; Asheville, North Carolina; and Kauai Island, Hawaii.

Final configuration

CatBoostClassifier: 500 estimators, learning rate 0.05, depth 8, subsample 0.75, regularization 1, class weight 5, and random seed 1.
